title: Vision Transformer Finetuning Benefits from Non-Smooth Components
claim: Components with high plasticity (non-smooth) produce large, varying rates of change and larger gradients, enabling faster descent than smooth components.
layout: 2x2 grid; smooth left vs non-smooth right; top 3D surfaces, bottom loss contours
description: A 2x2 grid of plots contrasting a smooth component (left column, LayerNorm) with a non-smooth one (right column, attention). The top row shows 3D surface plots of rate of change, ||f(x)-f(y)||/||x-y||, over a two-dimensional input perturbation plane, colored with viridis and a shared colorbar. The LayerNorm surface is low and flat and mostly blue-purple. The attention surface is tall, jagged, discontinuous, and yellow-green. The bottom row shows 2D loss-landscape contour maps with a white SGD trajectory ending in a blue star. On the left the path is a tiny stub in a flat magenta landscape. On the right the path is longer and descends into a dark low-loss basin. A magma colorbar sits on the right. The eye goes first to the colorful jagged attention surface.
caption: Non-smooth components facilitate finetuning. We illustrate the benefits of a high plasticity during the finetuning of ViT-Base on Cifar10 (values normalized to [0, 1]). Smooth modules like LayerNorm (top left) have low and steady rates of change, resulting in low plasticity (see Definition 1). This constrains the gradient norms during the optimization, leading to a slow descent on the loss landscape (bottom left). In contrast, the rates of change of non-smooth components, such as multihead attention (top right), are large and vary a lot, resulting in high plasticity and gradients of high magnitude. This allows the exploration of the loss landscape and a faster descent towards (local) minima (bottom right).
abstract: The smoothness of the transformer architecture has been extensively studied in the context of generalization, training stability, and adversarial robustness. However, its role in transfer learning remains poorly understood. In this paper, we analyze the ability of vision transformer components to adapt their outputs to changes in inputs, or, in other words, their \emph{plasticity}. Defined as an average rate of change, it captures the sensitivity to input perturbation; in particular, a high plasticity implies a low smoothness. Our theoretical analysis and extensive experiments -- over $1,000$ finetuning runs on large-scale vision transformers -- showcase that this perspective provides principled guidance in choosing the components to prioritize during adaptation. A key takeaway for practitioners is that the high plasticity of the attention modules and feedforward layers consistently leads to better finetuning performance. Our findings depart from the prevailing assumption that smoothness is desirable, offering a novel perspective on transformers' functional properties. The code is available at https://github.com/ambroiseodt/vit-plasticity.
